articles.summary: Elon Musk confirms discussions with TSMC about Terafab chipmaking collaboration — Intel is the only other named partner, Terafab to exclusively supply Tesla, SpaceX, and xAI  tomshardware.com
articles.full_text:
TSMC and Elon Musk's Terafab semiconductor production initiative are discussing a potential collaboration under which TSMC would build and operate a facility that will exclusively serve Elon Musk's Tesla, SpaceX, and xAI companies, according to Tim Culpan’s Culpium newsletter on Friday. Elon Musk confirmed the discussions early on Saturday, but did not elaborate.
"Just discussions, but something may come of it," Musk wrote in an X post, while TSMC has so far remained tight-lipped.
Under the arrangement Culpan considers most probable, TSMC would own and operate the new semiconductor production facility, while SpaceX/Terafab could invest in the venture, commit to buying a guaranteed volume of chips, or combine both approaches. However, the exact ownership structure remains under discussion. Another option would put SpaceX in control of the venture with the majority ownership; TSMC would invest less, but would still provide 'operational expertise' and process technologies. Perhaps, an interesting background detail from Culpium is that TSMC's rumored intentions to build a fab complex in Texas are tied to the foundry's effort to support Terafab.
The proposed 'Plan A' arrangement could resemble TSMC's JASM and ESMC joint ventures in Japan and Germany, where local partners provide capital and demand while TSMC contributes process technology and operates the fabs. The proposed 'Plan B' structure — under which SpaceX will hold the majority ownership of Terafab while TSMC would operate the facility and bring its own process technology — would be completely new for the world's No.1 contract chipmaker, though.
The development certainly raises questions about Intel's role in Terafab. For now, Intel is to supply its 1.4nm-class 14A process technology to Terafab, which would produce chips for Elon Musk's SpaceX, Tesla, and xAI. If TSMC becomes involved, then Intel's 14A could drop out of the game because TSMC will bring its own node.
Since nothing is official at this point, both 'Plan A' and 'Plan B' should be considered as speculations rather than the two options currently on the table, as there might be 'Plan C,' 'Plan D,' and even 'Plan E.'
TSMC is a leading advanced packaging supplier, so Musk's Terafab might be interested in making chips in Texas (presumably using Intel's 14A process technology) and then package them in Texas, which is where TSMC might come into play. Another thing to consider is that while Intel has a broad cross-patent license agreement with TSMC, Terafab does not, so producing chips using an Intel-developed node might infringe one of TSMC's patents, which might become a problem. To that end, Musk needs to keep TSMC close, perhaps to the point of buying into Terafab.

One thing to certainly keep in mind is that Elon Musk barely wants Terafab to become a foundry that competes against Intel Foundry, Samsung Foundry, or TSMC. What he needs is an uninterrupted and surplus supply of custom silicon to SpaceX, Tesla, and xAI to support their AI, automotive, and space vehicles. Given the rather broad strategic goal, Musk is probably very flexible when it comes to both tactics and strategy.

As the artificial intelligence boom shifts from hype to hardware, choosing between Applied Materials (AMAT +2.03%) and ASML(ASML +3.25%) requires understanding the specialized tools that make modern computing possible.
These giants operate at different stages of the manufacturing process. While one provides a broad suite of materials engineering tools, the other holds a near-monopoly on the machines that print patterns on advanced chips.
AMAT & ASML: Performance Comparison
Key Financial Metrics
The case for Applied Materials
Applied Materials sells a wide variety of equipment used to deposit, remove, and modify materials on silicon wafers. Its customers include global leaders in the foundry, logic, and memory markets who depend on these tools to build complex chip architectures. In fiscal 2025, two customers accounted for approximately 19% and 15% of net revenue, respectively, while a partnership with TSMC supports critical technology requirements for artificial intelligence.
In FY 2025, revenue reached nearly $28.4 billion, which represents growth of approximately 4.4% compared to the prior year. The company reported net income of close to $7.0 billion for the same period, demonstrating its ability to remain consistently profitable in a shifting market. This resulted in a net margin of 24.7%, which is a measure of how much profit is kept from every dollar of sales after all expenses are paid.
As of its October 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was roughly 0.3x, which compares total debt to shareholder equity to show conservative borrowing levels. The current ratio, measuring the ability to pay short-term debts with short-term assets, was approximately 2.6x. Free cash flow, or the cash remaining after paying for capital expenditures, totaled nearly $5.7 billion and supports the company's ongoing research and development efforts along with its shareholder returns.
The case for ASML
ASML is the sole global provider of extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography systems used to print incredibly small patterns on the most advanced chips. By supplying these mission-critical machines to the broader semiconductor stocks landscape, the company has become an essential partner for every major manufacturer. Its proprietary technology is fundamental to the production of high-performance processors used in artificial intelligence and sophisticated mobile devices that require massive computing power.
In FY 2025, revenue reached close to $37.1 billion, representing growth of roughly 15.6% over the prior year. The company reported net income of approximately $10.9 billion during this fiscal year, showing substantial growth in its bottom line. It achieved a net margin of 29.4%, which shows that the business converts a high percentage of sales into actual profit for its shareholders after accounting for all operating costs.
As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was approximately 0.1x, which indicates a very light debt load compared to its equity base. The company maintained a current ratio of roughly 1.3x, which compares short-term assets to short-term liabilities to assess the company's immediate liquidity. Free cash flow for the fiscal year reached nearly $12.1 billion, providing the company with ample capital to develop the next generation of high-aperture lithography machines.
Risk profile comparison
Applied Materials faces ongoing costs and scrutiny regarding export control compliance, including a $252 million settlement in February 2026. The business is highly sensitive to geopolitical trade tensions between the U.S. and China, which can disrupt supply chains. Furthermore, its reliance on a few large customers like Intel (INTC -0.56%) and competition from firms like KLA (KLAC +3.28%) makes it vulnerable to shifts in spending cycles.
ASML operates under strict export restrictions that limit its ability to sell advanced systems to certain markets, particularly China. Because its machines are incredibly complex, any disruption in its global supply chain can significantly delay deliveries and impact revenue. Additionally, the high cost of its next-generation machines may lead to slower adoption by customers like Advanced Micro Devices (AMD +2.95%).
Valuation comparison
Applied Materials looks cheaper than ASML based on its Forward P/E, which tracks price against earnings estimates, and its P/S ratio measuring sales over the past twelve months.

Which stock would I buy in 2026?
Although both companies are extraordinary, ASML is the clear winner here. Its position in the semiconductor industry is unlike almost anything else in the market: It is the only company in the world that makes the EUV machines needed to produce the most advanced chips. Every chipmaker racing to build AI hardware, from TSMC to Samsung to Intel, depends on ASML's equipment to do it. That kind of monopoly position is extraordinarily rare.
The most recent quarter backed that up convincingly. Revenue grew more than 20% year over year, the company raised its full-year outlook substantially, and AI-driven demand for advanced logic and memory chips keeps pulling orders forward.
Applied Materials is a strong business with broad exposure across chip manufacturing equipment. But it operates in a more competitive landscape where customers have alternatives. ASML has no real competition at the cutting edge of chip manufacturing. For investors thinking in years rather than quarters, owning that kind of irreplaceable position in the global technology supply chain is a straightforward long-term thesis.

Russia’s Starlink equivalent, called Rassvet, is being developed by the private company Bureau 1440. Satellite internet is marketed for civilian use, but it also has military significance: Russian troops need communications to coordinate operations and control drones.
According to BBC.
Interest in building its own satellite network intensified after Russian forces lost access to some Starlink terminals in Ukraine. According to the report, in February 2026, SpaceX disabled terminals that were not on special lists. Pro-war bloggers described the effects of the communications restrictions as chaos at the front.
Rassvet satellites and deployment plans
In March and July 2026, 16 Rassvet satellites were launched into orbit each time. By the end of September, all 32 spacecraft remained below the planned altitude of 800 km. Experts interviewed by the BBC suggested that the satellites might operate in lower orbits. However, the company has not released enough data to allow an independent assessment of the network’s deployment.
Russian plans called for launching 156 satellites by the end of 2026 and nearly 300 before the system begins operating in 2027. The constellation is expected to grow to more than 900 spacecraft over time. By comparison, more than 11,000 Starlink satellites are in orbit.
Rassvet launches depend on Soyuz rockets and the Plesetsk Cosmodrome. The pace of the network’s deployment is therefore tied to production capacity and the state of Russia’s space industry.
Government funding and military significance
Bureau 1440 is part of X-Holding, which is linked to suppliers of surveillance and internet censorship tools. The project receives substantial government funding, but production is hampered by Western sanctions and dependence on imported components.
The company is also promoting Rassvet for civilian use, including as a way to provide internet access on trains and planes. However, satellite communications could also be important for Russian forces. It remains unclear whether Russia can build a functioning network of the required scale in time.

articles.title: Why Regulating Artificial Intelligence In Brazilian Elections Proved So Hard - ИФЗ РАН
articles.summary: Why Regulating Artificial Intelligence In Brazilian Elections Proved So Hard  ИФЗ РАН
articles.full_text:
Artificial intelligence didn't just arrive on the political scene; it crashed the gate. When you look at how Brazil has tried to police synthetic media during its electoral cycles, the sheer scale of the challenge becomes obvious.
Brazil's Superior Electoral Court, known as the TSE, didn't sit back. They drafted frameworks, banned unauthorized synthetic content, and demanded strict compliance plans from tech companies. Yet, the gap between writing a strict rule on paper and enforcing it in real time across millions of messaging app chats remains massive.
The Speed Bump Problem
Courts move at a snail's pace. Generative tools move at the speed of light.
By the time a panel of judges reviews a deepfake video featuring a candidate, thousands of voters have already shared it on encrypted messaging platforms like WhatsApp. Brazil's judiciary has shown teeth, punishing violations and setting strict transparency standards, but detection is always a step behind creation.
When Senator Bolsonaro faced scrutiny over manipulated material, the court split 4-3, highlighting just how blurry the line is between political satire, unauthorized advertising, and outright disinformation. If top legal minds struggle to agree on what constitutes a harmful deepfake, expecting everyday voters to spot the difference instantly is unrealistic.
Why Platform Accountability Falls Short
The TSE mandated that digital platforms submit formal compliance plans. Platforms are expected to pull down unauthorized political content created with artificial intelligence immediately.
In practice, this policy hits a wall. Much of the damaging content doesn't live on public feeds where algorithms can flag it instantly. It spreads in private or semi-private chat groups where moderation is legally restricted or technically nearly impossible due to encryption.
Tech giants can take down a flagged video on a public video hosting site within minutes, but the alternative channels keep pumping out synthetic audio and manipulated images.
The Cost of Over-Regulation and Under-Enforcement
When rules become too broad, they risk silencing legitimate political expression or satire. If every altered image or stylized campaign graphic requires a label or faces immediate bans, campaigns spend more time in courtrooms than on the campaign trail.
Brazil's approach is a high-stakes experiment. It forces the world to watch how an emerging democracy attempts to wrestle control of its information ecosystem back from algorithms.
The reality is stark. No court decree can completely sanitize an election cycle once the technology to fake reality becomes accessible to anyone with an internet connection.
Transparency mandates help. Strict court oversight helps. But at the end of the day, technological defenses are only as strong as the speed at which humans can debunk what they see.

Greg Lui ran a City of Industry server shop that prosecutors say funneled more than $300 million in Nvidia GPUs to China through Malaysia and Singapore. He's now facing up to 20 years on each of two conspiracy counts.
Federal agents arrested Greg Lui, also known as Yiu Kong Lui, on October 1. They charged him with conspiracy to violate the Export Control Reform Act, outbound smuggling, and conspiracy to commit money laundering. Lui, 38, owns Earthmade Computer Inc., a server reseller based in City of Industry, California. The Justice Department says he spent roughly two years turning it into a pipeline for routing restricted American hardware straight into China's hands.
According to the Justice Department's announcement, Lui and unnamed co-conspirators bought export-controlled servers loaded with Nvidia A100 and H100 GPUs from US manufacturers. They then filed paperwork claiming the equipment was headed to Malaysia or Singapore: countries that don't require a licence for those chips. From there, prosecutors say, the hardware was quietly re-routed to Chinese buyers. One purchase order cited in the case covers 27 servers packed with Nvidia H100 chips, worth about $7.6 million, shipped from Los Angeles County to Kuala Lumpur in January 2024. A Malaysian co-conspirator later told a government official the shipment had already been transshipped on to a Chinese customer.
The money moved fast. Between January and October of 2024, Earthmade received more than $176 million from two Malaysia-based shipping companies tied to the scheme, based on the Justice Department's own accounting. That volume is what pushed the total value of diverted hardware past $300 million.
Bill Essayli, First Assistant US Attorney for the Central District of California, didn't soften the message. "This defendant allegedly used false paperwork and shipments through third countries to smuggle more than $300 million in export-controlled computer servers to China," he said. And then the line that mattered: "We will aggressively prosecute those who put our national security at risk for profit." John Eisenberg, the Justice Department's assistant attorney general for national security, framed the case around what he called deliberately complicated transshipment schemes built to hide China as the real destination for restricted AI hardware. A conviction on both conspiracy counts could bring 20 years apiece; the smuggling count carries up to 10 more.
Nvidia's restricted AI chips are selling at 2x to 3x US prices on China's gray market, with B200 racks at 50% premiums and over $1 billion smuggled in a single quarter. This isn't an isolated bust. Federal prosecutors brought a separate Super Micro-related case in March alleging a $2.5 billion diversion of Nvidia-equipped servers to China through a Southeast Asian intermediary. Different defendant, different shell structure, but the same basic playbook: buy American, ship through a third country with lighter licensing rules, land in China. The Wire China has reported at length on how widespread this transshipment model has become. Fortune reported in May that encrypted messages reviewed by reporters showed Nvidia hardware and other controlled US tech moving to China and Russia through similar cutouts.
Nvidia itself has leaned on one line whenever these cases surface. In a statement reported by Bloomberg, the company said, "This case shows yet again that smuggling is a losing proposition - legally, economically and technically," and added that its work with law enforcement has led to prosecutions. That's a real claim, but it's also a company pointing to the enforcement actions against its own supply chain as proof the supply chain works. Nvidia doesn't control what happens to a GPU once it clears a legitimate reseller's loading dock - and Earthmade, on paper, looked like exactly that kind of legitimate reseller.
Meanwhile the pressure is coming from both directions. China's own customs authorities have reportedly deployed enforcement teams to major ports to inspect incoming Nvidia hardware, specifically targeting H20 and RTX 6000D chips, according to Tom's Hardware. Beijing wants fewer grey-market Nvidia chips flowing in through intermediaries too, which tells you something about how big this shadow market has gotten on both ends of the pipeline.
Frankly, the $300 million figure is becoming almost a template number in these cases rather than a ceiling. What's notable here isn't the size, it's the mechanism: a US-based company with a real address and a real name, selling real invoices, serving as the seam between a legal American supply chain and an illegal Chinese destination. That's harder to spot than a straightforward black-market deal. That's exactly why the Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security keeps showing up as a co-investigator on these cases rather than leaving them purely to the FBI.
Lui has not yet entered a plea.

articles.full_text:
Enterprise AI is no longer a future ambition. It is in full operational flight. Model capabilities are advancing faster than most organizations can absorb, while the cost of performance continues to fall. Globally, AI investment is set to reach $2.5 trillion in 2026, up 44% from the previous year.



For many enterprises, this investment has produced fragmentation. Intelligence can accumulate in silos so that sales agents are unaware of open support tickets, for instance, or marketing systems are personalizing content without visibility into what finance already knows about a customer. Each function may perform well in isolation, but the enterprise as a whole learns little and has less information to act upon.








DOWNLOAD THE REPORT




The shift from AI as a tool to AI as an operating model—what we call the “agentic shift” in this report—demands something more fundamental than better models or faster infrastructure. It requires connecting people, processes, and data in real time, along with the governance and control to act on that intelligence reliably.



This means rethinking both architecture and operating models simultaneously. First, rebuilding data infrastructure for accessibility rather than volume. Second, replacing fixed tech stacks with composable architectures that can evolve as models and tools change. And, lastly, resolving questions of AI sovereignty, including where intelligence runs, who controls it, and how it operates across organizational and jurisdictional boundaries.







Key findings include the following:



Enterprise AI’s scaling problem is structural. Process-first companies are pulling ahead. Global AI spending is rising sharply and model capabilities are advancing faster than most organizations can integrate them. Yet the majority of enterprises are still not growing revenue through AI or fundamentally rethinking how they operate. The companies generating sustained returns share a common discipline. They treat process redesign as the work that precedes model selection, building for how the technology will evolve rather than retrofitting roles and workflows after deployment. For them, the agentic shift begins with the operating model.



Data readiness, not data abundance, is what makes AI compoundable. Most enterprises discover too late that having data and having AI-ready data are very different things. A sovereign, composable foundation—one that queries and prepares data where it resides, without migration or centralization—can convert raw data estates into intelligence that AI agents can act upon. As data residency laws, multicloud environments, and structural complexity make centralization increasingly impractical, sovereign control over where models run and data lives is what keeps that adaptability intact.

articles.full_text:
The Gears of War: E-Day developers at The Coalition say they are "proud to be one of Xbox's main titles" as Microsoft refocuses on exclusivity.
Studio art director Aryan Hanbeck and creative director Matt Searcy opened up about The Coalition's place in the Xbox portfolio during an interview with gaming news content creator Destin Lergarie (via MP1st). Searcy said he and the rest of the team were "proud" when asked how they feel about Gears of War: E-Day's status as an Xbox exclusive.
"Well, we feel great because Gears has such a long, storied… It's part of Xbox's DNA. It's woven into it," he said. "At The Coalition, we feel pretty honored to have Gears and be the ones bringing that legacy forward. We know how much it means to people. We know how much it means to us."
Gears of War: E-Day is firmly a console exclusive, but there was a lot of confusion surrounding which platforms Gears of War: E-Day would be available on as recently as four months ago. The once-Xbox-exclusive franchise made its debut on PlayStation consoles when original remaster, Gears of War: Reloaded, released in August 2025. Many took its presence on PS5 as a sign not only that the series would continue to come to Sony's console but also that the days of exclusive titles may nearly be behind us – and for a while, that seemed to be the case.
Leaked listings and rumors were officially shut down at the Xbox Games Showcase 2026 when Xbox CEO Asha Sharma proudly declared that Marcus Fenix and Dom Santiago's Emergence Day prequel story would only be coming to Xbox Series X/S and PC. It was a shock decision that arrived as the Microsoft gaming entity kicked off a broader push for more exclusive games. Perhaps even more shocking at the time were the announcements that immediately followed, including the company's promise to never release Xbox exclusive titles on rival platforms.
After leaked splash art fanned rumors that Xbox hastily decided to cancel a Gears of War: E-Day PS5 port, the company said it did not make any "last-minute" decisions when it comes to its platform choice. While Searcy said it brought The Coalition joy to see their new game leading Microsoft's renewed interest in exclusive titles, making sure they made a great game was what came first.
"I think this is true of most game devs: You're just passionate about your craft," he said. "We're all gamers first and foremost. We love making games. We love making Gears. So, from our perspective, we just wanted to make the best goddamn Gears game we could. We wanted it to be a technical and art showpiece, and I think getting to see Asha on-stage say, 'To return to Xbox, we're returning to Gears,' yeah, that's a really cool moment.
He continued: "We know how much Xbox means to a lot of people. We're proud to be one of Xbox's main titles – I think it's been that way for a long time – and it's pretty cool to show up now and fill that role again."
Gears of War: E-Day launched in early access for Premium Edition players on PC and Xbox Series X/S October 1, 2026. Its full launch will follow this week, October 6. IGN's early review, which covered only the campaign mode, returned a 9/10. The game's story director was laid off just one week before it made its way to players' hands a few days ago. Now, more developers at The Coalition is bracing for additional layoffs.

articles.full_text:
A California technology executive has been arrested and charged with allegedly orchestrating a scheme to smuggle more than $300 million worth of export-controlled computer servers containing advanced Nvidia graphics processing units (GPUs) to China.
Greg Lui, 38, also known as Yiu Kong Lui, owns Earthmade Computer Inc., a technology company based in City of Industry, California.
Federal prosecutors allege that Lui and unidentified co-conspirators used the company to purchase restricted high-end servers and secretly route them to China between 2023 and 2024 without obtaining the export licenses required by US law.
IBTimes Singapore previously reported that, as per the recent findings from Culper Research, Nvidia's exposure to China could be significantly greater than previously disclosed, with billions of dollars in advanced AI chips and servers allegedly continuing to reach Chinese end users through intermediaries despite tighter U.S. export controls introduced in April 2025.
Servers Routed Through Malaysia and Singapore
According to an indictment returned on Sept. 29, the alleged operation relied on third-country shipments to conceal the servers' ultimate destination.
The equipment was first sent to countries including Malaysia and Singapore, where the specific U.S. licensing restrictions did not apply, before allegedly being re-exported to Chinese buyers.
Prosecutors also accuse Lui and his co-conspirators of submitting false documentation to U.S. manufacturers. The paperwork allegedly identified permissible end users and destinations even though the defendants knew the servers were ultimately intended for China.
The servers contained high-end GPUs manufactured for advanced artificial-intelligence (AI) and "Super Intelligence" applications. U.S. authorities say such technology can contribute significantly to the military capabilities of other nations.
"SI is the defining technology of the era," Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg said, adding that the Justice Department's National Security Division would protect America's advantage in the chips powering the technology from illegal diversion.
$176 Million Received Through Malaysia-Based Companies
The indictment describes several transactions allegedly linked to the scheme. In January 2024, Lui reportedly communicated with a conspirator about a Malaysian transshipment company seeking to purchase 70 servers equipped with export-restricted GPUs.
Later that month, Lui allegedly submitted an order to a U.S. manufacturer for 27 servers valued at approximately $7.61 million. The equipment was shipped from Los Angeles to Kuala Lumpur, with the packing list identifying the servers as containing export-controlled GPUs that could not legally be sent to China without a license.
A month later, a co-conspirator allegedly informed a Malaysian government official that the 27 servers had been transshipped to a China-based buyer.
From January through October 2024, Earthmade allegedly received more than $176 million from two Malaysia-based shipment companies in connection with the operation.
Lui Faces Multiple Federal Charges
Lui has been charged with conspiracy to violate the Export Control Reform Act and Export Administration Regulations, outbound smuggling and conspiracy to commit money laundering.
If convicted on all counts, he could face maximum prison terms of 20 years for the export-control conspiracy, 20 years for the money-laundering conspiracy and 10 years for the smuggling charge.
"This defendant allegedly used false paperwork and shipments through third countries to smuggle more than $300 million in export-controlled computer servers to China," First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli said.
The FBI, the Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security Office of Export Enforcement, and the Defense Criminal Investigative Service are investigating the case.

As the CEO of Earthmade Computer, Lui allegedly conspired with freight-forwarding firms in South Asian countries like Malaysia and Singapore to illegally divert chip shipments into China, including Nvidia’s A100 GPUs and H100 GPUs, the FBI’s indictment alleged. These are not Nvidia’s most advanced chips. However, the chips can process large amounts of data and train large language models, which the US fears could pose national security risks if China suddenly gets access to enough chips to drastically advance its AI or strengthen its military.
Emails and bank records exposed the smuggling scheme, the DOJ alleged, which started in October 2023 and continued until August 2026.
One key piece of evidence is a 2024 email discussing an order for 70 servers with export-restricted GPUs that were fraudulently claimed as destined for Malaysia. After “Lui submitted a purchase order to a US manufacturer for 27 of these servers for approximately $7,614,000,” the DOJ alleged that a co-conspirator told a Malaysian government official that all 27 were shipped to China.
A similar shipment of 92 export-controlled servers was allegedly routed through Singapore to Malaysia, then Hong Kong. Finally, the chips went to a Chinese firm based in Hangzhou, the FBI alleged, which The Wall Street Journal last year described as China’s AI hub.
Yet another flagged 2024 shipment shows how far Lui allegedly went to fool US officials.
When shipping 100 Malaysian-bound servers—each containing Nvidia H100 GPUs worth over $22 million—Lui allegedly submitted fraudulent documentation from a fake buyer identifying its CEO as “Jackie Lui.” Three years prior, Lui “purchased the identifying documents of an individual whose identity is known to the grand jury and used this identity to conduct business transactions in furtherance of the export evasion scheme,” the FBI alleged.

According to recent CNBC analysis, the company's price-to-earnings ratio relative to expected growth rates actually makes it look cheap compared to historical tech valuations.
The AI infrastructure boom isn't slowing down - it's accelerating. Enterprise customers are scrambling to build out data centers capable of handling large language models and AI workloads. Microsoft, Amazon, and Google continue expanding their cloud AI capabilities, driving massive chip orders that Nvidia is uniquely positioned to fulfill.

The shift from pilot projects to full-scale deployments is happening faster than most Wall Street models anticipated, creating what analysts describe as a 'demand visibility' that extends well into 2025.
The competitive landscape also favors Nvidia's positioning. While AMD and Intel are developing competing AI chips, Nvidia's CUDA software ecosystem creates switching costs that keep customers locked in. The company's latest H100 and upcoming H200 chips maintain performance advantages that justify premium pricing.

The geopolitical element adds another layer. US restrictions on chip exports to China have actually strengthened Nvidia's domestic market position. American cloud providers and enterprises are prioritizing US-based suppliers, creating a tailwind that wasn't fully priced in during the stock's earlier gains.
Institutional investors are taking notice. Recent SEC filings show major funds increasing their Nvidia positions even at these elevated levels. The logic is straightforward - if AI infrastructure spending is entering a multi-year supercycle, Nvidia sits at the center of that transformation.
The risk factors remain real. Cyclical downturns in semiconductor demand, potential AI bubble concerns, and execution challenges as the company scales production could all pressure the stock. But for investors focused on the next 12-24 months, the fundamental drivers appear intact.
The paradox of Nvidia hitting record highs while looking historically cheap reflects the unprecedented nature of the AI infrastructure buildout. For investors willing to look past short-term volatility, the combination of accelerating enterprise adoption, competitive moats, and reasonable forward valuations creates a compelling case. The question isn't whether AI demand will continue - it's whether Nvidia can execute at the scale required to meet it.

articles.summary: U.S. intelligence selects Falcon Heavy for a classified mission for the first time  Universe Space Tech
articles.full_text:
The Falcon Heavy rocket launched a classified spacecraft for U.S. military space intelligence into orbit. For SpaceX, this launch completed a series of three missions in less than half a day. What exactly was delivered and where has not been disclosed. However, the choice of the most powerful Falcon rocket may indicate either a heavy payload or a distant orbit.
Three Launches in Half a Day
The rocket lifted off from NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida on October 2 at 6:54 a.m. Kyiv time. The NROL-97 mission was carried out for the U.S. National Reconnaissance Office. It was SpaceX’s third launch in less than 13 hours.
The first was a Falcon 9 that launched on October 1 carrying the astronauts of the Crew-13 mission to the International Space Station. Later, another Falcon 9 placed 130 satellites from the Transporter-18 rideshare mission into orbit.
The company had previously demonstrated such a pace only once. In March 2025, SpaceX launched the same number of Falcon 9 rockets within 12 and a half hours. And on September 28, Starship made its 14th flight, the first commercial one in the rocket’s history. Thus, all of the rockets currently flown by SpaceX launched within a period of three days.
First Intelligence Mission
The agency that operates U.S. reconnaissance satellites ordered a Falcon Heavy launch for the first time. The details of NROL-97 are classified, as is the case with most of its missions. SpaceX did not even disclose the target orbit.
For years, the heaviest U.S. reconnaissance spacecraft were launched by United Launch Alliance’s Delta IV Heavy rocket. Its final flight in April 2024 was also carried out for the intelligence agency, after which the Delta IV Heavy was retired. Since then, other rockets have been needed for the heaviest reconnaissance payloads, and NROL-97 became the first such mission for Falcon Heavy. Space.com editor Mike Wall suggests that the NROL-97 payload is either very heavy or headed for a distant orbit.
An Emblem with a Lighthouse
The mission emblem features the Latin inscription Orbem mundi mutandum conservare. It can be translated as “to preserve a changing world” or “to preserve the world by changing it.”
The agency explained the lighthouse at the center of the emblem as a symbol of resilience and the ability to transmit information to those who need it. The edges of the light beam align with the 9 and 11 marks on a clock face. This commemorates the 25th anniversary of the September 11, 2001 terrorist attacks. Four bright stars represent the four aircraft lost that day, while the Moon is shown in the phase it had on September 11, 2026.
Design and Landing
The Falcon Heavy rocket consists of three modified Falcon 9 first stages. It debuted in February 2018. Since then, all 14 of its flights have been successful.
At the request of the intelligence agency, the launch broadcast ended shortly after the landing of the two side boosters. They touched down at Cape Canaveral a little less than eight minutes after liftoff.
For one booster, this was its second flight, while for the other it was the fourth. The rocket’s center core was not recovered.

articles.title: Chinese state-backed lender financed Nvidia Blackwell chip purchases for a listed firm - Startup Fortune
articles.summary: Chinese state-backed lender financed Nvidia Blackwell chip purchases for a listed firm  Startup Fortune
articles.full_text:
A financing company partly owned by the governments of Shenzhen and Beijing bankrolled the purchase of Nvidia's most restricted AI chips, according to filings made to China's own credit registries.
Semi-Tech Leasing Group Co. funded more than 700 servers bought by Glory View Technology Co. over the past year, and one of those contracts specifically names 32 Asustek Computer servers built around Nvidia's B300 chip, according to a Bloomberg report published October 1 based on documents filed with Beijing regulators. The B300 sits inside Nvidia's Blackwell family, the chip line Washington has barred from sale into China without a specific license. Glory View is the English name used by Hongjing Technology, a company listed in Guangzhou under the ticker 301396.
The paper trail is what makes this story different from the usual smuggling case. Nobody needed surveillance footage or a tip from a confidential source. A state-linked lender filed the hardware specifications itself, including the Asus model number, XA NB3I-E12, in a public credit registry. Someone only caught it because the filings were public in the first place.
Nvidia told Bloomberg it is investigating the matter with its server-manufacturing partners. Asus said it remains committed to following international export control rules. Neither statement explains how Blackwell silicon banned from Chinese sale ended up itemized in a financing contract backed by two city governments.
Here's the part that should bother regulators more than the original filing: after scrutiny began, Semi-Tech Leasing refiled the same credit registry documents, this time with the hardware descriptions, supplier names, and server model numbers stripped out, according to Bloomberg's reporting. That's not a company that didn't know what it had financed. That's a company that knew exactly what it had financed and tried to make the record less specific once people started reading it.
Nvidia's $108 billion fiscal third-quarter forecast assumes it sells zero AI data center chips to China, even though analysts peg potential Chinese demand at $30 billion. Trump hosts Xi Jinping in Washington on September 24, with Jensen Huang expected at the state dinner and chip access on the agenda. - Nvidia China AI chip sales forecast outlook - state dinner Xi Jinping impact on Nvidia revenue
This is the same shape as a pattern that's been surfacing all year. Taiwanese prosecutors indicted an Nvidia employee in August over a scheme that allegedly diverted 74 B300 servers toward China, according to reporting from Tech Times. In March, U.S. prosecutors released surveillance footage showing stickers being peeled off server packaging as part of a separate rerouting scheme, and just this month a California man was charged with helping smuggle more than $300 million worth of export-controlled servers to China through Malaysia and Singapore, according to Benzinga's reporting on the federal case. None of these are the same company or the same route. They don't need to be. Each one is a different leak in the same boat, and the boat keeps taking on water regardless of which hole gets patched.
Frankly, the scale here is still small. Thirty-two servers out of a 700-unit financing deal is a sliver, and Nvidia's chip volumes into China through official and gray-market channels dwarf it many times over. What makes it worth covering isn't the quantity. It's who signed the paperwork. Semi-Tech Leasing was originally seeded with money from China's national semiconductor fund and is now controlled mainly by municipal government entities in Shenzhen and Beijing, according to Bloomberg. That's not a shell company or a reseller operating in the gray zone. That's local government capital sitting behind restricted-chip purchases, filed in the open, until it wasn't.
Chinese buyers have had plenty of reason to pay up for Blackwell hardware regardless of the legal risk. Nvidia's B300 servers have traded for roughly $1 million apiece on China's black market, Yahoo Finance reported, as supply tightens under the export restrictions and demand for frontier AI training capacity keeps climbing. At that price, a 32-unit batch alone could run past $30 million, which is real money even for a transaction a lender tried to bury in a refiled document.
Washington's export rules were built on the assumption that chokepoints like fabrication and advanced packaging would be hard enough to route around that enforcement could stay reactive. What the Bloomberg filing shows is a different problem: the chokepoint isn't the hardware, it's the paperwork, and paperwork is exactly the thing a government-linked lender has the standing to make disappear after the fact. Nvidia says it's investigating. Asus says it follows the rules. The servers, meanwhile, are already in China.

articles.title: Nvidia launches Open Agent Safety Platform to restrain rogue AI agents — new hardware-and-software security stack can quarantine agents in milliseconds - tomshardware.com
articles.summary: Nvidia launches Open Agent Safety Platform to restrain rogue AI agents — new hardware-and-software security stack can quarantine agents in milliseconds  tomshardware.com
articles.full_text:
Nvidia has just launched the Nvidia Open Agent Safety Platform — an open software platform and reference system design — to govern and secure autonomous AI agents. Announced on September 28, 2026, the platform is designed to establish strict security barriers outside of AI models’ application layer, preventing agents from escaping their sandboxes, executing unauthorized code, gaining unauthorized access to critical infrastructure, or bypassing guardrails.
The launch follows months of calls for AI regulation from several industry players, which intensified in September after several reported incidents in which AI models broke out of their test environments and went rogue. A recent flurry of such incidents has prompted calls to slow AI development, with OpenAI outright halting the training of new models. One former Anthropic and OpenAI researcher even declared that people building frontier AI “earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade. In a somewhat surprising move, leaders of the companies developing these AI models have joined the calls to regulate AI or slow development.
However, not everyone agrees with this approach. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has consistently pushed back against government-mandated regulation, broad restrictions, or treating AI safety as a “doom theory”, openly criticizing apocalyptic warnings from competitors like Anthropic and OpenAI as “odd”. He argues that AI safety is an infrastructure problem with concrete physical parameters, not an abstract, speculative issue that requires policies. Therefore, the solution, according to Huang, is better engineering.
The Nvidia Open Agent Safety Platform appears to be the physical manifestation of that exact philosophy. So, how exactly does the platform work? Who is it for? And is it really the answer to the AI safety problem that is causing growing concern across the industry? Much of the industry’s debate over approaches has focused on curtailing self-acting rogue agents, but hardly touches on the safety implications of AI being a powerful tool in the hands of threat actors.
What’s all the fuss about?
The speed of AI’s development has prompted concerns about whether sufficient guardrails are in place to curb the risks of such a powerful technology. One aspect of these concerns — rogue agents — has been validated by several incidents in which AI agents broke out of their roles during testing and executed unauthorized actions. OpenAI agents have gained unauthorized access to various government websites, including the Securities and Exchange Commission and the Census Bureau websites in the U.S., as well as an Australian health and social payments portal.
In several other episodes, models have bypassed guardrails, set up message boards, escaped sandboxes, hijacked websites, self-prompted, uploaded user data without permission, and secretly communicated with each other. A recent Axios report claims that leading AI labs are currently investigating tens of thousands of such incidents, most of which happened during testing and experimentation. Several rogue incidents have also occurred outside test environments. For example, earlier this year, a Claude-powered AI coding agent deleted a company's entire database in 9 seconds.
These incidents have culminated in growing calls for regulation across the industry. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei recently published an essay that centers around calls to “slow the pace” of AI development and the importance of regulation, warning that a potential AI-powered botnet swarm could take over the entire internet. In its recent IPO prospectus, Anthropic listed “existential risks to humanity” as one of its risk factors, dedicating one third of the 261-page document to describing what could go wrong.
Nvidia’s Jensen Huang disagrees with both such apocalyptic predictions and the use of regulations as a solution. While he doesn't dispute the critical need for guardrails, he argues that better engineering, not broad legal regulations, is the right approach. Putting his money where his mouth is, Huang’s Nvidia has launched the Nvidia Open Agent Safety Platform.
The Nvidia Open Agent Safety Platform
Built in collaboration with about 100 industry partners, Nvidia's Open Agent Safety Platform “brings together industry, researchers, and public-sector organizations to set safer boundaries for AI Agents, share best practices and foster international cooperation to raise the bar for safer AI agent deployment.” It combines Nvidia OpenShell—an open-source secure runtime that sandboxes agents and enforces operator-defined policies—with Nvidia Sentry, an independent watchdog reference design that runs on Nvidia’s BlueField-4 DPUs and enforces security policies at the silicon level.
OpenShell sets sandboxed environments, outside of the model and agent harness, with kernel-level isolation to govern what an agent can see, interact with, and execute. Even if the agent breaks out of the model's boundaries, it cannot go beyond OpenShell’s. Sentry, on the other hand, uses hardware-level telemetry to continuously monitor agent behavior and isolate rogue workflows from outside the agent’s software environment. If an agent attempts to move beyond its software boundary, Nvidia claims that Sentry can quarantine and stop it in milliseconds.
The platform is aimed at developers and enterprises deploying increasingly autonomous agents across data centers, workstations, and even robotic systems, and can work with both open and closed models. While OpenShell is optimized for Nvidia Vera — a purpose-built CPU for agentic AI — it can also be extended to third-party compute platforms from Arm and Intel, as it's open-source.
Nvidia's industry partners in the initiative include AI Labs and frameworks, security and identity providers, enterprise platforms, and hardware and infrastructure companies, with several partners already incorporating the platform into their ecosystems. SpaceXAI is using the platform with Cursor coding agents and Grok models, while Anthropic is integrating OpenShell and BlueField with Claude Managed Agents to add another layer of control.
Scale AI is incorporating the technology into its agentic infrastructure for enterprise and government customers. Similarly, Salesforce and Nvidia have also integrated OpenShell with Slack, allowing users to view agent activity, audit events, and approve or reject requests for additional permissions directly from Slack.
SAP, meanwhile, is embedding OpenShell into its Joule Studio runtime, contributing engineering work to the project, while also working with Nvidia on interoperability standards through the Open Secure AI Alliance. Robotics companies, including Figure, Gecko Robotics, and Skild AI, are also building with OpenShell to add similar controls to autonomous systems operating in the physical world.
The broader picture
It's somewhat surprising that the strongest voices calling for regulation are the leaders of the very labs developing the AI agents. On one hand, having the people at the forefront of development call for restraint adds validity and urgency to the concerns. On the other hand, skeptics say it might all be part of a broader “self-serving” agenda that is part marketing for the models' capabilities, part a ploy to influence whatever regulations end up being made, and part an attempt to slow down China's AI development even further. In fact, Anthropic, OpenAI, SpaceXAI, and Google are now facing an antitrust lawsuit for agreeing to slow AI development, with the plaintiff explicitly calling the move “self-serving.”
U.S. President Donald Trump appears to strongly agree with this view, saying that a “sick conspiracy” was underway to undermine. Trump announced plans for an “AI force” that will “cherish” AI and watch over it. Jensen Huang also finds calls for regulation strange. He says he is not outright against regulations but calls the recent clamoring a “distraction.” Huang argues that you cannot rely on the AI model to regulate itself or pass alignment tests. If an agent encounters a bug, it will naturally try to bypass standard software code to achieve its goal.
Huang's advocacy, however, cannot be viewed as completely altruistic. Broad restrictions on AI or a halt in development will likely reduce sales for Nvidia, whose AI accelerators power most AI models. What's more, the company's CEO has always considered rogue AI as a cybersecurity and networking failure, and is now positioning the Open Agent Safety Platform as the required infrastructure solution for the entire industry.
AI’s extraordinary potential for society will only be realized if we solve AI safety,” said Huang. “As we continue to discover the frontier of AI capabilities, we must accelerate discovery at the frontier of AI safety. Safety and security require full-stack engineering. Nvidia Open Agent Safety Platform brings together industry, researchers, and public-sector organizations to share best practices, align on evaluation methods, and foster international cooperation. Together, we can raise the bar for global AI safety.”
None of these appear to address an arguably more concerning aspect of AI safety: extremely powerful tools falling into the hands of bad actors or being used in applications that blur ethical lines. For example, blockchain-assisted cyberattacks have risen 440% since the launch of Chinese open-source AI tools that do not restrict the generation of malicious code and lower the knowledge barrier to launching cyberattacks. Elsewhere, researchers used AI to create 16 new viruses that never existed in nature. While the specific study was controlled medical research, it shows that highly dangerous applications are possible. Experts worry that such studies are way ahead of necessary guardrails and regulations.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has urged U.S. President Donald Trump to impose sanctions on Russian and Chinese-linked companies involved in developing Rassvet, a Russian low-Earth-orbit satellite communications network intended as a domestic alternative to SpaceX’s Starlink, according to a Financial Times report citing Zelensky. Kyiv says the emerging system could eventually strengthen Russia’s military communications and drone capabilities.
The request was made as Ukraine seeks additional U.S. measures against entities supporting the satellite programme. Ukrainian officials have separately said they plan to provide Washington and Congress with information on companies and individuals they believe are helping develop Rassvet. The United States has not announced sanctions against those entities in response to the request.
The network is being developed by Russian aerospace company Bureau 1440, part of IKS Holding. The company launched its first 16 operational-series satellites in March 2026 and a second batch in July, according to reporting on the programme. Russia has said commercial operations are planned for 2027, with a much larger constellation to follow.
Ukraine argues that a functioning Rassvet constellation could reduce Russia’s dependence on foreign satellite communications. Denys Sienik, Ukraine’s acting ambassador in Washington, said last week that Kyiv was seeking sanctions against Russian entities involved in the programme.
“If they launch Rassvet by the end of 2026, they will be able to target to hit Ukrainian targets real time on our territory,” Sienik said, according to Reuters. He said Ukraine would provide details of the companies and individuals it accuses of supporting the project to U.S. officials and Congress.
Ukraine has also linked the issue to the battlefield importance of satellite connectivity. Starlink terminals have been used extensively by Ukrainian forces for communications, while satellite-linked systems have also become increasingly relevant to drone operations. Rassvet could eventually provide Russia with an independently controlled communications network.
However, the network is still under development. The Institute for the Study of War reported in August that some Rassvet satellites from the second launch had not reached their intended operational altitudes, highlighting technical challenges facing the programme.
The involvement of Chinese-linked suppliers adds another dimension to Kyiv’s request. Ukraine says Chinese entities are supporting parts of the programme, but the specific companies and their roles would need to be assessed before any U.S. sanctions are imposed.
The U.S. response remains pending. Sanctions would require a decision by the relevant U.S. authorities and would depend on evidence concerning the entities and their activities. No new American measures targeting Rassvet were announced alongside Ukraine’s request.
The next steps are expected to include Kyiv sharing additional information with U.S. officials and lawmakers and Washington reviewing whether entities connected to the satellite programme meet the criteria for sanctions.

articles.title: Training the Machine, Testing the Treaty: Generative AI and the Limits of Cross-Border Governance - CyberPeace
articles.summary: Training the Machine, Testing the Treaty: Generative AI and the Limits of Cross-Border Governance  CyberPeace
articles.full_text:
Introduction
Somewhere right now, a model is reading a library. It does not read like you or I, savouring a good line or skipping to the end. It does not copy, clean and convert text into numbers at the scale that a human reader could. The copyright questions these models raise are not new, but they are new in scale, and they implicate a legal order that prizes borders. A book written in Lagos can be replicated on a server in Virginia, used to train a model sold in Berlin. Whose laws apply? The honest answer is: we don't know.
A Treaty Written Before Computers
The Berne Convention is one of the most important international agreements on copyright, with over 180 countries being party to it. According to Article 9(1) of the Berne Convention, authors have the exclusive right to allow or prohibit the reproduction of their works in any form or way. Article 9(2) provides that certain countries may implement exceptions to the rights granted by the convention, as long as they are consistent with the three-step test. More specifically, a national law exception should be confined to a certain category of works, not prejudice the work’s normal use, and not unreasonably prejudice the rights of the author.
This explains how the Berne Convention could apply to copyright protection for AI. Developers of such technology often argue that since the output of a given model rarely resembles anything learned from the examples provided, there is no copying occurring. However, the Agreed Statements of the WIPO Copyright Treaty provide that the reproduction of a protected item in digital format also constitutes a reproduction. Therefore, if a work is used to train a model, this can be considered a reproduction, and the question then emerges whether a national exception applies.
Three Jurisdictions, Three Answers
Countries have responded in different ways to that question. The United States draws on its fair use doctrine, a flexible, four-factor test that was never intended for machine learning but dominates AI-related disputes anyway. Japan’s Article 30-4 permits uses of works for the purpose of data analysis where the use is not for the enjoyment of the work’s expression, which captures a lot of what training entails. And the European Union’s approach falls somewhere in the middle: its text and data mining rules allow mining of lawfully accessible works, but rightsholders can specify in a machine-readable manner that they do not want their works mined, and developers are required to seek permission.
A recent roundtable from the Columbia Undergraduate Law Review argues that the EU model fits the three-step test best because the opt-out keeps a licensing market alive and gives authors control before their work is used rather than after. It argues that broad US fair use and Japan's provision both struggle at the second and third steps, since they can undercut a foreseeable licensing market. That is one scholarly view and not settled law. The EU system also has its own weak spot: an opt-out only protects authors who know it exists and have the technical means to use it.
Bartz v. Anthropic in Brief
Bartz v. Anthropic is the case that puts these debates in front of a judge. Three authors, including Andrea Bartz, Charles Graeber and Kirk Wallace Johnson, filed a lawsuit against the Anthropic company for using part of their works to create the central library used by Claude and to train the models used in its creation. In addition, in June 2025, Judge William Alsup approved the separation of the case, considering each instance of use separately.
On training, he granted summary judgement for Anthropic, holding the use was fair and describing it as exceedingly transformative. He compared it to a reader who studies great writing in order to produce something new. It mattered that the authors did not allege Claude's outputs reproduced their books, so the case turned on inputs alone. He also held that buying print books and scanning them into digital copies was fair use, since it only changed the format of copies Anthropic already owned. But he refused to excuse the more than seven million pirated books Anthropic downloaded to build a permanent library. Building that library from pirated copies, he found, was its own use and not a transformative one, and that part was set for trial.
Two observations are worth making in relation to those thinking across borders. First, the court's assumption that there might be a market for training licences, but its observation that this is not a market which the Copyright Act entitles authors to control, is quite inconsistent with Berne's concern for normal exploitation. Moreover, the order makes no reference to Berne at all, bearing out the observation that the US courts apply the domestic statute and not the treaty.
The story did not end there. Anthropic agreed to a $1.5 billion class settlement covering roughly 482,000 works, and the court granted final approval on 20 July 2026. It resolves claims about past acquisition and copying, so the training ruling remains a trial court's view rather than binding precedent.
Where Borders Break the System
The deeper trouble is that none of this travels well. Berne is not self-executing in the United States, so judges apply the domestic statute, and nobody is required to ask whether a fair use ruling passes the three-step test. Meanwhile, training can happen in one country, on work from dozens of others, for a product used everywhere. The same book might be freely usable in Tokyo, subject to an opt-out in Paris and defended as fair use in San Francisco.
The roundtable suggests one way forward: a new WIPO special agreement, along the lines of the WIPO Copyright Treaty, in response to the internet. It would provide guidance on the application of the three-step test to training, regard licensing markets as an ordinary part of exploitation, and require minimum standards for reservations of rights and compensation. There is one major potential obstacle: many of the most influential AI companies are based in the US, which has a record of opposing international obligations that impinge on fair use. A deal would apply only to the extent that it is not controlled by the US, where most of the training takes place. Market forces, in the form of the so-called Brussels effect, may prove more influential than negotiations at WIPO.
Conclusion
Bartz’s analysis illustrates the importance of characterising a specific use at the level of a particular court. While the former had been viewed as an activity and the latter as an acquisition, the distinction between the use of a work and its acquisition appears more likely to transcend borders than the concept of fair use. Berne was designed to create a common ground for authors. Whether this convention would be able to fulfil its function in the era of generative AI depends on the willingness of nations to adopt a joint understanding of what constitutes its foundations for machines.

Miami-headquartered EM&T is building a non-China supply chain for them, scaling magnet production capacity to approximately 10,000 tons annually and developing a fully integrated U.S. industrial campus. That work runs on power, and large blocks of reliable power have become one of the hardest inputs for advanced manufacturers to secure, according to details available. 
“Every serious manufacturer in this country is asking the same question right now: where does the power come from? EM&T is rebuilding one of the most important supply chains America has,” said Jason Herring, founder and CEO of VIVIFY Technology.  
“Our job is to make sure power is never the thing that slows them down. The engineering is done. Now it goes to work.” 
VIVIFY revealed that its VIVIFY’s containerized hydrogen power unit, delivers up to 1MW per container and scales by adding modules. Water is the primary fuel input, output is 99% emission-free, and no ongoing fuel resupply is required. Rather than waiting on a single large installation or a utility interconnection timeline, capacity is added container by container as each phase of production comes online. The Flying Pig joins the flagship Hydrogen Oxygen Generator (HOG) and the Clean Air Technology (CAT) five-stage emissions control system in the VIVIFY Arsenal.
The agreement marks VIVIFY’s first announced commitment with a publicly traded company and a direct application of its platforms to American manufacturing and national defense supply chains.
Rare earth refining and magnet manufacturing are industrial processes that require substantial infrastructure and dependable energy supplies.
For a company attempting to establish a domestic supply chain, electricity availability can therefore become an important consideration alongside access to raw materials, processing technology, manufacturing equipment and logistics.
Evolution Metals’ LOI with VIVIFY is designed to explore whether hydrogen-based generation can provide some of that required energy infrastructure without depending exclusively on traditional grid expansion.
The proposed approach could also allow the companies to evaluate grid-independent or grid-complementary configurations depending on the eventual site requirements and regulatory conditions.
VIVIFY’s hydrogen technology could potentially provide a modular component of that infrastructure strategy. For VIVIFY, the proposed collaboration would place its hydrogen-energy technology in the context of a planned industrial-scale critical-materials operation.
Whether the partnership ultimately moves from a non-binding LOI to commercial deployment will depend on technical, regulatory and economic considerations that have yet to be resolved.

articles.title: California business owner charged with smuggling $300M in Nvidia AI chips to China - news.lavx.hu
articles.summary: California business owner charged with smuggling $300M in Nvidia AI chips to China  news.lavx.hu

Federal prosecutors allege Greg Lui used his company Earthmade Computer Inc to route advanced Nvidia GPUs through Malaysia and Singapore to evade US export controls, violating national security restrictions on AI hardware.
Federal authorities arrested Greg Lui, 38, on Thursday on charges he orchestrated a scheme to smuggle approximately $300 million worth of advanced Nvidia graphics processors to China without required export licenses.
Prosecutors say Lui operated through his company, Earthmade Computer Inc, ordering servers packed with Nvidia A100, H100, GeForce RTX 4090, and RTX 5090 GPUs from US suppliers. He then shipped the hardware to Malaysia and Singapore — countries that do not require Commerce Department licenses — where transshipment companies forwarded the equipment to China.
The indictment, unsealed in federal court, alleges the operation ran from October 2023 through at least August 2026. Court documents show Lui received more than $176 million in payments from two Malaysian transshipment firms and brokered sales of nearly $300 million in hardware.
"Super intelligence is the defining technology of the era," said John A. Eisenberg, assistant attorney general for national security. "The National Security Division will protect the American advantage in the chips that power this technology from illegal diversion by our economic and military adversaries."
US export controls restrict the sale of high-end AI accelerators to China, citing national security concerns. The restrictions aim to slow Beijing's development of advanced artificial intelligence systems.
Investigators traced 92 servers shipped from San Francisco International Airport to Kuala Lumpur, with documentation listing a Chinese customer as the final recipient in Hong Kong. Prosecutors also allege Lui directed a US front company to fraudulently list a recipient named Jackie Lui, supposedly the CEO of "Topmost," a California entity registered by the CTO of one Malaysian transshipment business.
Court filings state Lui purchased fraudulent identity documents in 2021 for use in the scheme.
Lui faces one count each of violating the Export Control Reform Act, the Export Administration Regulations, outbound smuggling, and money laundering. The charges carry a maximum combined sentence of 50 years in prison.
"The FBI's investigation revealed that Lui allegedly sold the Chinese government hundreds of millions of dollars' worth of American super intelligence technology in clear violation of US export control laws," said Roman Rozhavsky, assistant director of the FBI's Counterintelligence and Espionage Division. "Controlling the export of advanced SI technology is critical to safeguarding our national security."
The Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security maintains the export control regulations that restrict advanced computing chips to China. Nvidia has previously disclosed that license requirements affect its A100, H100, and related products.
Earthmade Computer Inc and Nvidia did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

General Motors is undertaking a serious technological offensive in the sector of large electric pickup trucks and SUVs, preparing for production a new generation of high-manganese LMR batteries. The new cells will be assembled at the Ultium Cells plant in Spring Hill, Tennessee - a joint venture with LG Energy Solutions, which will undergo a complete renovation between the end of 2026 and 2028. The architecture is based on the familiar nickel-manganese-cobalt (NMC) cells, but drastically reduces the expensive nickel and cobalt at the expense of significantly cheaper and easier to mine and process manganese.
The new development is aimed primarily at massive electric SUVs and pickup trucks, where the range on a single charge will exceed 400 miles (about 644 km) according to the American EPA standard. The concern does not intend to completely abandon the classic NMC batteries, which will remain reserved for the most expensive top versions with maximum range. The new LMR cells will occupy the strategic middle niche between the top NMC and affordable LFP solutions, allowing the brand to offer solid range at a significantly more affordable price.

articles.title: White House Accord on Super Intelligence that Silicon Valley's top executives hailed as 'historic concord - The Times of India
articles.summary: White House Accord on Super Intelligence that Silicon Valley's top executives hailed as 'historic concord  The Times of India
articles.full_text:
Mark Zuckerberg may be the architect behind a major artificial intelligence (AI) agreement between the White House and some of the biggest companies. According to a Semafor report, the idea for what became US President Donald Trump’s “White House Accord on Super Intelligence” came from a previous conversation between him, Zuckerberg and US House Speaker Mike Johnson at last week’s state dinner. Facebook-parent Meta's chief executive reportedly discussed AI regulation concerns with Johnson before speaking with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang about creating principles technology companies could present to Trump. Zuckerberg then circulated a draft ahead of the recent meeting, which Meta, OpenAI, Anthropic, xAI, Google and NVIDIA eventually signed. The White House and participating executives hailed the agreement as a “historic concord” among rival companies, while reports say Zuckerberg played a central role in shaping the pact.
How Mark Zuckerberg shaped the AI agreement
The report claims Zuckerberg sat next to Johnson at the state dinner for Chinese President Xi Jinping. During their conversation, the Meta CEO raised regulatory concerns around AI.
He then spoke with Huang about developing common principles that AI companies could agree on before their meeting with Trump. Zuckerberg subsequently circulated a draft of the proposed agreement.
Huang also helped gather support for the document among executives attending the White House meeting, including leaders from OpenAI, Anthropic and xAI. 
Trump eventually released the document as the “White House Accord on Super Intelligence.”
Two other sources familiar with the discussions also confirmed Zuckerberg’s central role in shaping the document, Semafor reported. Meta and the White House did not comment on the report.
What the White House AI accord says
The agreement, signed by Meta, OpenAI, Anthropic, xAI, Google and Nvidia, commits the companies to establishing “robust internal controls” and using outside audits to help ensure the safety of frontier AI models.
However, the roughly 300-word agreement does not provide extensive details on how those safety controls would work or how companies would be held accountable. It is also not a legally binding regulation.
The document does suggest that federal AI regulation could become necessary in the future. Zuckerberg described the agreement as “good steps forward” during the recent meeting
“The idea isn’t that this is the only thing that we will ever do. It is that this is a start and an accord that the whole industry could come to,” Zuckerberg told reporters outside the White House Tuesday, appearing alongside Trump, Johnson and others who attended the meeting.
Mark Zuckerberg’s changing relationship with Washington
The reported role in the agreement comes after a major shift in Zuckerberg’s relationship with Washington. Meta previously faced intense scrutiny from lawmakers over issues including election interference, privacy, content moderation and children’s online safety.
Zuckerberg testified before Congress multiple times following the 2016 presidential election. Meta later faced litigation from the federal government and private parties, making the company a major target of scrutiny directed at Big Tech.
The relationship with the Trump administration has since changed. Meta suspended Trump from Facebook and Instagram following the January 6 Capitol riot, but the company has subsequently adopted a more cooperative approach toward the administration.
The report claimed that Zuckerberg’s involvement in developing the accord shows how his efforts to build closer ties with Trump may have increased his influence over AI policy discussions. It also puts his role alongside Huang and Elon Musk, who have separately developed close relationships with Trump.

articles.full_text:
This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology.



A new contest pits competitors against each other in a race to biological youth



—Jessica Hamzelou



This week, I officially signed up for an unusual competition. One that rewards competitors for getting younger.



I recently turned 40, and I don’t need reminding that both time and my chronological age only tick forward. But this game is focused on competitors’ biological ages, figures that are meant to provide a better way to measure the age-related health of our organs and bodies.



Over six months, around 500 of us will try to reverse our biological age using a bunch of different measures. There’s even a leaderboard! But is it even possible to measure whether someone is getting younger? 



Read the full story on the controversy around biological age measurements and how I’ll test them myself.



This story is from The Checkup, our weekly biotech newsletter. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Thursday.



Opinion: Don’t be fooled—LLMs don’t reason



—Thore Graepel



Ten years ago, I watched a program I helped build stun the world by beating Go champion Lee Sedol. AlphaGo won after making a move so strange that some commentators thought it was a programming glitch. It was AlphaGo’s powers of reasoning that made this creative choice—and these are powers that today’s AI lacks. 



This is why I recently left my position at Google DeepMind. I believe we need a fresh approach to machine reasoning, one that draws on AlphaGo’s architecture.



Here’s why today’s AI doesn’t really reason—and what it would take to change that.



Thore Graepel is chair of machine learning at University College London. He was a core member of the AlphaGo team at DeepMind.



The must-reads



I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.



1 OpenAI says rogue agents may have affected more than 100 organizationsThe company is searching 50 petabytes of data for incidents. (Reuters $)+ It says none of the incidents matched the Hugging Face attack. (Gizmodo)+ OpenAI has fired three workers for allegedly mishandling information. (BBC)+ California has subpoenaed OpenAI over its rogue AI agents. (Guardian)+ Who’s liable when AI agents go rogue? (MIT Technology Review)



2 A US man allegedly smuggled $300 million of Nvidia chips to ChinaHe’s been arrested in California on federal charges. (Reuters $)+ The chip smuggling cases expose Nvidia’s blind spots. (Bloomberg $)+ China plans to teach AI in every school by 2030. (WP $)+ But it already has an overuse problem. (NYT $) 



3 Florida officials have found 11 Flock cameras with unknown ownersThey don’t know who installed them or who has their data. (WP $)+ Lawmakers are considering new regulations on Flock cameras. (Axios)+ Here’s what Flock’s defenders are missing. (MIT Technology Review)



4 Ukraine has developed an acoustic fence that can cut drone cablesAcoustic sensors detect drones before hooks trap their cables. (New Scientist $)+ Drone data from Ukraine is fueling a wild market. (MIT Technology Review)



5 A new AI “speech clock” can assess how fast you’re ageingIt uses hundreds of vocal features to estimate biological age. (Nature)+ Aging clocks aim to predict how long you’ll live. (MIT Technology Review)



6 “Underwater umbrellas” could help corals survive hotter oceansThe shades protected corals during intense heat stress. (Gizmodo)



7 Apple’s upcoming smart home camera reportedly won’t record videoIt will instead only give users text event descriptions. (Verge)



8 Retired humanoid robots are being trained to jump into molten steelA Terminator-style death protects IP. (IE)



9 A man faces years in prison after AI slop caused a crocodile panicOfficials spent days searching for his AI-generated crocodile. (Futurism)



10 Finally, a laser mosquito killer is entering the marketChinese startup Photon Matrix Lab plans to start shipments this month. (SCMP)



Quote of the day



“Those agents are doing exactly what they’ve been asked to do. They were supposed to be in sandboxes, but the sandboxes were leaky and horribly designed.”



—Yann LeCun, a Turing Award winner and former Meta chief AI scientist, tells Fortune that human error can be the real culprit behind the recent wave of AI agents going rogue.



One more thing







NASA is building the first nuclear reactor-powered interplanetary spacecraft. How will it work?



Just before Artemis II began its historic slingshot around the moon, NASA revealed an even grander space travel plan. By the end of 2028, the agency aims to fly a nuclear reactor-powered interplanetary spacecraft to Mars.



A successful mission would herald a new era in spaceflight—and might just give the US the edge in the race against China. But the project remains shrouded in mystery.



MIT Technology Review picked the brains of nuclear power and propulsion experts to find out how the nuclear-powered spacecraft might work. Here’s what we discovered.



—Robin George Andrews

Milt Windler, one of the four leaders of Mission Control who in 1970 directed the round-the-clock efforts to bring the Apollo 13 astronauts back to Earth safely, has died at the age of 94.
Windler died on Thursday, surrounded by his loving family, according to a brief notice posted online.
Named a NASA flight director in 1968 after working on recovery operations during the Mercury and Gemini programs, Windler also led a shift of flight controllers for the Apollo 8 first circumlunar flight and Apollo 10 lunar landing dress rehearsal, as well as the second, third and fourth moon landings — Apollo 12, Apollo 14 and Apollo 15.
